terms.gloss: lie down at table, take one’s place on the dining couch
evidence: Cic. Mur. 74: cotīdiānīs epulīs in rōbore (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: The Romans ate lying on couches, propped on the left elbow; accumbe is what a host says where we say “sit down”. In summō accumbere, to take the top place.

terms.gloss: be lying at table (the state, where accumbō is the act)
evidence: Plaut. Bacch. 81b: ut lepidus cum lepidā accubet
Cic. Cat. 2.10: accubantēs in convīviīs (Lewis & Short)

terms.gloss: take one’s places at table (of the whole company)
evidence: Cic. Att. 5.1.4: discubuimus omnēs praeter illam (Lewis & Short)
terms.comment: Especially frequent from the Augustan age on (Lewis & Short).

phrases.latin: Age accumbe igitur. Cedo aquam manibus, puere, appōne hīc mēnsulam.
phrases.english: Come on then, take your place. Boy, bring water for our hands, put the little table here.
You, Sagaristio, take the top place.

sources: Lewis & Short: accumbo · Lewis & Short: accubo · Lewis & Short: discumbo
